t: as it is said: “and had I eaten a sin offering today, would it have been good in the eyes of the Lord?”. These are Aaron's words to Moses on the day his two sons, Nadav and Avihu, died: he could not eat the sin offering although eating offerings is a positive commandment, because his sons died that day. From here it is learned that the mitzvah of mourning applies on the first day alone. But the mitzvah of mourning itself is learned from the verse “for her he may defile himself” (Leviticus 21:3), which requires the kohen to become impure for his relatives when they die, and therefore also to mourn for them (Kinat Soferim on Sefer ha-Mitzvot positive commandment 37; Lechem Mishneh; and see below 2:6; and see Radbaz, who explained differently).

which is the day of death and the day of burial. But if the burial is on a different day, there is no mourning by Torah law, neither on the day of death nor on the day of burial (Aruch ha-Shulchan 399:1, but see Lechem Mishneh).
although it is said in the Torah. When Joseph and his brothers took our father Jacob to his burial.
the Torah was given and the halachah was renewed. And we do not determine halachah from what was practiced before the giving of the Torah.
and the seven days of feasting. After the wedding (see Hilchot Ishut 10:12).
the golel. The cover of the grave.
the things that a mourner is forbidden. Detailed below 5:1.
when the child died. The first son born to him from Bathsheba, who was decreed to die (see II Samuel 12:14-20).
those executed by the government, whom they do not allow to be buried. Who were killed by the authorities, who do not allow their bodies to be returned for burial.
even if they have not despaired of stealing them. Since theft is not common, mourning should not be delayed for this.
once they have despaired of searching. When they have given up the search for his body, they begin counting seven and thirty days.
they do not count for him. They do not begin counting seven and thirty days.
to another country. To another city.

and anyone who did not live thirty days etc.. When it is not known for certain whether nine months of pregnancy were completed and he did not live thirty full days, we are in doubt whether he is defined as a viable child or a stillborn, and we are lenient not to mourn for him (Kesef Mishneh).
even if he died on the day he was born, they mourn for him. Because he stayed in his mother's womb a full nine months, he is considered viable even if he died the same day.
a nine-month child. Who stayed nine months in his mother's womb.

and an eight-month child. Who is known for certain to have been born after eight months in his mother's womb, and therefore is considered a stillborn even if he lived more than thirty days (see Hilchot Shabbat 25:6).
cut up. Whose limbs were severed in his mother's womb and emerged in order, for example the hand emerged and then the leg, and so on.
scrambled. Whose limbs were severed in his mother's womb and emerged out of order (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 3:5).

and they do not occupy themselves with them. With eulogy, funeral procession and the like; but in caring for the body and the needs of the bier and burial they do occupy themselves for them (Tur Yoreh De'ah 344, and similarly wrote Responsa of the Rashba 1:563). It is possible to explain that they do not even occupy themselves in caring for the body and its bier as is done for other dead, but only bury (see below, halachah 11, 4:1, Hilchot Yom Tov 1:23).
all those executed by the government. For example, one who rebels against the king or insults him (see Hilchot Melachim 3:8).
and they do not withhold from them anything. Of the things done for the honor of the dead.
and their property goes to the king. See also there 4:9.

but for all those executed by the court, they do not mourn... until the flesh decays. Because those executed for sin by the court do not have their sins atoned for at the time of death but only when the flesh decays, so at the beginning of mourning, which is the sealing of the grave, they are not fit for mourning, and therefore their mourning was postponed entirely (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 6:8; and see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 13:6).
but onenim, for aninut is only in the heart. They are permitted to grieve for them, since heartache is not defined as an act of mourning.
the minim. The heretics (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7-8; the "min" mentioned here is a general term for all the types of heretics mentioned there).

and the meshumadim. Those who transgress deliberately and in rebellion against the commandments of God, even one who transgresses a single sin in order to spite (Hilchot Teshuvah there 3:9, Hilchot Rotzei'ach 4:10).
and the informers. Those who hand over their fellows or their property to gentiles or violent people (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:12).
stand over him in a row. After the burial of the dead, the comforters stand in rows on leaving the cemetery and pass the mourners one by one and comfort them (see below 13:1-2).
the blessing of mourners. Things said in the mourner's house (below 12:7).
and anything that is an honor to the living. Things by which his relatives are honored.
not one who climbed to the roof and fell and died. Perhaps he fell by accident and did not intend to take his own life.

and they saw him go up immediately in anger or in distress. That immediately after he threatened that he intended to climb to the top of the roof in order to fall from it, they indeed saw him go up to the roof in his anger or from his distress.
but if they saw him etc.. And they had not heard from him earlier that he intended to take his own life.
his sword. His blade.
he is in the presumption of all the dead. And we do not regard him as one who took his own life.
and by their words. By the words of the Sages (see Rulings and Opinions).
his married wife. Married to him, excluding his betrothed (as below, halachah 3).
that he does not become impure for his brother and sister from his mother. As below, halachah 12.
nor for his married sister. As below, halachah 10.
his son or brother who came from a maidservant or from a gentile woman. Who was born to a Canaanite maidservant or to a gentile woman and follows his mother, and is a slave or a gentile.
and likewise one who converted, he and his sons, or was freed, he and his mother. After converting or being freed he is considered like a newborn and is not related to his parents or brothers.

and not an onen. An onen is a person whose close relative for whom he is obligated to mourn has died; on the day of death he is an onen by Torah law, and on the night after the day of death he is an onen by rabbinic law. An onen is forbidden to offer sacrifices and to eat sacrificial food and second tithe (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:5-7, Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 2:9-10). [Note: in the words of the halachic authorities the term "onen" refers to a person whose dead lies before him and has not yet been brought to burial; the laws of this situation are explained in the Rambam below 4:6 and in Rulings and Opinions there.]
he mourns with them. When a relative dies for whom they are obligated to mourn.
in their presence. When he is with them.
his son's brother. A brother of his son by another mother.
his son's mother. After he divorced her.
he overturns his bed. He turns over his bed (as below 5:18).
or her son. By another man.

and likewise anything similar. When the relationship of the deceased to his relatives is not one of blood kinship but a relationship through marriage, he is not obligated to mourn with his relatives for them.
in what cases does this apply. That it is a mitzvah to become impure, and that they make him impure against his will.
since they are not warned about impurity. As below 3:11.
by rabbinic law. By the words of the Sages.

they made her like a met mitzvah etc.. Although the prohibition of a kohen's impurity is from the Torah and mourning for his wife is only rabbinic, since they equated her to a met mitzvah, the prohibition of a kohen's impurity is set aside for her burial (Radbaz; for the law of a met mitzvah see below 3:8).
all those for whom we said they do not mourn. Above 1:9-11.
until the grave is sealed. Until they cover the grave.
the disqualified. Challalim, born of a divorcee who married a kohen.
mamzerim. Born of forbidden sexual relations (except one born of a niddah; see Hilchot Issurei Biah 15:1).
his disqualified wife. Who is forbidden to him and whom he must divorce.
one who heard that her husband died and married etc.. The law is that she is forbidden to both husbands and needs a get from both (see Hilchot Gerushin 10:5).

a challalah. A woman who was forbidden to the priesthood and had relations with a kohen, or a woman born of a kohen's marriage to a woman forbidden to him (Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:1). This applies only if she was disqualified after he was born; but if she was disqualified before he was born, this son is a challal and is not warned against becoming impure for the dead (as below 3:11).

even though she is married to a kohen. Although she retained the sanctity of the priesthood regarding eating terumah and the like, he does not become impure for her (Tiferet le-Moshe Yoreh De'ah 373).
a bogeret. A girl who reached age twelve and a half, whose signs of virginity have diminished and who is no longer called a complete virgin (see Bavli Yevamot 60a-b, Hilchot Issurei Biah 17:13).
struck by a stick. Whose virginity was lost as a result of injury, not from intercourse.
one whose existence was by the hand of a man. Who had relations with a man.
who has not been to a man, except a betrothed woman. Who was betrothed to another and had not yet had relations.
also his brother and sister who are fit to inherit him. Only his brother and sister from his father are fit to inherit him (see Hilchot Nachalot 1:7).
the offspring that were mixed up. And it is not known for certain who the father of each child is.

and the son who is doubtfully a seven-month child of the later one or a nine-month child of the first. A woman who was divorced or widowed and did not wait three months before remarrying, and a son was born to her, and there is doubt whether he was born at seven months to the last husband or at nine months to the first husband.

and likewise any woman divorced with a doubtful divorce. Where there is doubt whether the divorce took effect, for example he threw her a get in the public domain and it fell midway between them (Hilchot Gerushin 5:12).
or with an invalid get. A get invalid by rabbinic law (see there 10:2), while by Torah law the woman is divorced.

for a limb from the living of his father. If a limb was cut from his father before he died, the kohen does not become impure for the burial of this limb (see below 3:1 for the explanation that a kohen is forbidden to become impure for a limb from the living).
nor for a bone of his father's bones. If a bone or limb is missing from his father after he died, he does not become impure for burying this bone.
and likewise one who gathers his father's bones. Who collects them from their first burial place to bring them for burial elsewhere.

even though the spine exists. The spinal column exists. And although a complete spine makes one who touches it impure like a whole corpse (see Hilchot Tumat Met 2:8), for the purpose of permitting a kohen's impurity it is not considered a whole body.

impurity for relatives is pushed aside and not permitted for all. The kohen's prohibition of impurity is set aside for the mitzvah of mourning for relatives, but this does not permit him to become impure for other people.
except for the six dead who are specified in the Torah. His mother and father, his son and daughter, his brother and his virgin sister (Leviticus 21:1-3).
or his wife. Whose impurity is rabbinic (above 2:7).
one who touches the dead. Who touched a corpse with his body (Hilchot Tumat Met 1:3).
one who overshadows. Who overshadowed the dead with his body, or the dead overshadowed him, or who stayed with the dead under one tent (there 1:10).
one who carries. Even though he does not touch the dead or the impurity itself with his body; likewise one who moves the dead or the impurity is considered a carrier and becomes impure (there 1:6-7).

or the other impurities that separate from the dead. For example a limb and flesh that separate from the dead. Likewise a limb cut from a living person makes impure like a corpse by Torah law and a kohen is forbidden to become impure for it (see there 2:1-4, and see above 2:14).
for it is said: “for a person he shall not defile himself”. All impurities separating from the dead whose prohibition is from the Torah are included in “person” (Radbaz).
and we already explained in Hilchot Tumat Met. Chapters 2-3.

all the things that make impure from the dead, by the Torah or by their words. If he became impure through things whose impurity is from the Torah, he receives lashes by Torah law; and for things whose impurity is rabbinic, he is given disciplinary lashes by rabbinic law (below, halachah 13).

if the kohen touched a grave, he receives lashes. Even though he did not touch the dead himself. Likewise if he overshadowed the grave or stayed with the grave under one tent, he receives lashes, since a grave makes impure even through a tent (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:15).

but he may touch garments that touched the dead. Garments that touched the dead make impure one who touches them with seven-day impurity, but this impurity is not from the Torah (see there 5:3-5). And although the kohen is warned also about rabbinic impurities (as below, halachah 13), he is permitted to become impure by this one even initially.
and likewise if he entered an impure tent into which the impurity entered. He entered a place that is impure because impurity in an adjacent room entered it through one of its doors or windows.

and we already explained all the tents into which impurity enters or from which it leaves. The places that are impure because the impurity enters them, and the places from which the impurity inside spreads to another place.
and the law of the projections and the protrusions. Tree branches that shade the ground and stones protruding from a wall that shade the ground (see Hilchot Tumat Met 13:2).
and all that bring the impurity. Under which the impurity spreads.
and those that interpose before the impurity. Things through which the impurity does not penetrate.
all of it in Hilchot Tumat Met. Mainly in chapters 12-19.
and there we explained. Hilchot Tumat Met 1:13.
that gentiles do not make impure by tent. For it is said regarding the war against Midian: “anyone who touches a slain person” (Numbers 31:19), and no tent is mentioned there.
and therefore their graves are pure. For the impurity of a grave is by the law of tent.

the time of a prostration, as we explained regarding the impurity of the Temple. For a person who entered the Temple pure and became impure must leave immediately, and if he stayed there for the length of time of a prostration lying on the ground (which is the time it takes to say the verse in II Chronicles 7:3: “and they bowed with their faces to the ground on the pavement and prostrated and gave thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His kindness is forever”), he is liable (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:21-23).
and separated. He let go of his contact with the dead.
he receives lashes for each and every one. Although he has not yet been purified from his earlier impurity, he receives lashes for becoming impure through a new act of impurity.
and returned and touched, and they had warned him. Before he touched.

for he is defiled and remains so as long as he has not separated. Since he did not separate from the impurity, there is no new act of impurity, and therefore he does not receive lashes (compare Hilchot Nezirut 5:16-17).

and the one who made him impure transgresses “and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block”. For anyone who strengthens the hands of transgressors or causes them to stumble transgresses this prohibition (Hilchot Rotzei'ach 12:14). But one does not receive lashes for this prohibition because it is a prohibition that includes many matters (a "general prohibition" - see Sefer ha-Mitzvot rule 9, Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:3).
if the kohen was unwitting and the one who made him impure was deliberate, the one who made him impure receives lashes. See also Hilchot Kilayim 10:31, Hilchot Nezirut 5:20.

from this you learn that he is liable for “he shall not enter” and liable for “he shall not defile himself”. Unlike an ordinary kohen, who in cases where he is forbidden to become impure and became impure transgresses only “he shall not defile himself”; a high priest transgresses also “he shall not enter.”
he entered the tent and sat there until the dead person died on him etc.. Compare Hilchot Nezirut 5:18.

or entered a shidah, teivah or migdal. Vessels which, if their volume is greater than forty se'ah, do not receive impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 3:2). And when their cover is closed, one inside them does not become impure (see Hilchot Tumat Met 21:1).
and his fellow came and removed the roof of the shidah over him. His fellow opened the cover of the vessel (compare Hilchot Nezirut there).

for impurity and entry come as one. In these two cases the impurity and the staying in the tent of the dead came at once, and therefore he receives lashes for both. But if the kohen entered in the ordinary way a tent that had a dead person in it, he receives one set of lashes, because entry and impurity do not come together, as from the moment he put in his nose or feet he was already impure, so his impurity preceded his entry (see there).
he became impure earlier etc.. For example, he touched the dead and became impure, and after he separated from the first impurity he entered a tent, and after he entered a person died there.
from the mouth of the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
a kohen and a nazir were walking on the road etc.. Compare Hilchot Nezirut 7:13.

for his sanctity is not an eternal sanctity. For unlike the priesthood, which is an intrinsic sanctity that applies to the kohen from birth, the sanctity of a nazir, even a lifelong nazir, stems from his acceptance of nezirut, and he also has the possibility of annulling it.
and the segan. The one appointed as deputy to the high priest (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:16).
the anointed for war. The one appointed to address the people at the time of war, anointed for this role with anointing oil (Hilchot Melachim 7:1).

let the anointed for war become impure and let the segan not become impure. Although the anointed for war ranks above the segan (see Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:19), regarding impurity the segan has priority, since one of his duties is to replace the high priest in the Yom Kippur service if he becomes impure (Bavli Nazir 47b).
the nasi. The head of the Sanhedrin or the king (Yad Peshutah, and see Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:1).

and likewise everyone is an onen for him. They are forbidden to eat sacrificial food and second tithe and cannot offer sacrifices, as with an onen (Yad Peshutah; for the explanation of the term onen in the Rambam's words see above 2:2 in the commentary).
the challalim. One born of a kohen's marriage to a woman forbidden to the priesthood (Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:5-6), and also one whose father is a challal (there halachah 14).
the court is not commanded to separate him, but his father must educate him in holiness. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 17:27-28.

a dead person occupies four cubits of his own for impurity. Out of concern that one might not know where the dead lies and might overshadow it, the Sages decreed impurity on an area of four cubits around the dead.
a rebellion lashing. Lashes by rabbinic law.

to a beit ha-peras. A field in which there was a grave and which was plowed, so that now bones of the dead are scattered throughout the field, and the Sages decreed corpse impurity upon it (see Hilchot Tumat Met 10:1).

to outside the Land. The Sages decreed corpse impurity on the soil of the lands of the gentiles because they are not careful to bury in one place and it is likely that the soil contains the bone of a dead person the size of a barley grain (there 2:16, Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 2:3).

by blood of tevusah. A revi'it of blood in which blood that left the dead person while alive is mixed with blood that left him after death; this blood makes impure by rabbinic law (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:13).

by the golel and the dofek. The golel is the cover placed over the grave, and the dofek are the stones that support the golel from the sides; they make impure by tent and by touch by rabbinic law (there halachah 15).
as we explained in Hilchot Tumat Met. 2:13-16, 5:11.

but if he entered a cemetery, he receives lashes by Torah law. For on entering the cemetery he overshadows the graves, and a grave makes impure by tent by Torah law (there 2:15). But if he does not overshadow the graves and is within four cubits of the graves, he is given disciplinary lashes (as explained at the beginning of the halachah), and outside four cubits it is permitted (Radbaz).

a kohen is permitted to become impure in a beit ha-peras or outside the Land for a matter of a mitzvah etc.. Since this is rabbinic impurity, the prohibition is set aside for the mitzvah of procreation or Torah study.
and likewise he may become impure by rabbinic impurity for the honor of people. For human dignity overrides a rabbinic prohibition (see also Hilchot Kilayim 10:29).

and likewise they step over coffins of the dead. Wooden coffins in which the dead are placed: if there is an open space of a handbreadth between the dead and the coffin lid, it is considered a tent that interposes against impurity, and when there is no open space of a handbreadth the coffin does not interpose and the impurity bursts through and rises. And although most coffins have an open space of a handbreadth, the Sages decreed impurity on all coffins because of the minority that have no such space (see Hilchot Tumat Met 12:6).
to meet kings. Out of respect for royalty.
even kings of the nations, in order to distinguish etc.. So that when Israel's honor is restored, he will be able to see the greatness of the reward of the kings of Israel.
because he saves from their hand. He saves his property from them.
they close. They shut the eyes.
and they plug his orifices. They stop up the orifices of the body so that wind does not enter them (Hilchot Shabbat 26:20).
and anoint him with kinds of spices. To remove a bad smell from him.
and they cut his hair. If it was too long.
in a cloth. A scarf, a garment.

so as not to shame the poor whose faces are blackened by hunger. At first they would uncover the faces of the rich and cover the faces of the poor because they turn black from hunger, and the living poor were ashamed that they were buried differently, so they enacted that the dead person's face always be covered (see Bavli Mo'ed Katan 27a).
and they carry. They bear.
it will snap. It will tear.
and he turns out to be delayed from the mitzvah. He will stop to fix his sandal and not be able to continue carrying the bier.
a koch. A grave.
and they return the earth and stones on top. They cover the dead or his coffin with earth.
and they may. They are permitted to.
and they mark the graves. They mark the burial place with lime so that kohanim can avoid grave impurity (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 5:1).
and they build a nefesh on the grave. A monument.

and a person shall not turn to visit the graves. Some explain that this refers to a prohibition of opening the grave (Radbaz; and see Responsa Chatam Sofer part 2, Yoreh De'ah 336). Others explain that this is the conclusion of the previous sentence, that one should not visit the graves of the righteous because their deeds are their memorial, and a person should turn and look to the memory of their good deeds (Kesef Mishneh based on Responsa Rivash 421). Others explain that it refers to a prohibition of turning to attain a spirit of impurity or communicate with the dead by visiting cemeteries (Yad Peshutah, and see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 11:13).
the goses. One in his last breaths (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Arachin 1:3).
and cool vessels. Cold vessels.
to a dripping candle. Whose burning may continue for some time.
and they do not place him on sand or on salt. They used to lay the dead on cool sand or salt so that he would not decay quickly from the heat of the cushions and pillows he lay on.
the one who closes. Who closes the eyes of the dead immediately when he dies.
and they do not bare the shoulder. Which is one of the mourning customs (below 8:3).
and they do not bring a coffin and shrouds into the house until he dies. So that the goses's mind not be unsettled, and so that they do not despair of praying for him (Yad Peshutah).
one whose dead lies before him. Who has not yet been buried.
eats in his fellow's house. And does not eat in front of the dead.
makes a partition. Between himself and the dead.
turns his face. Turns his body to the other side.
and either way. Even if the dead does not lie directly before him, and this dead person is his relative whom he is obligated to bury.

he does not recline and eat. He should not eat reclining, which is a manner of permanence and there is concern he may forget the needs of the dead (Shitah Mekubetzet Berakhot 17b); some explained that one may not recline because reclining is a manner of distinction (Rashi there).
and does not eat meat and does not drink wine. So that he not be drawn after them and become lax about the needs of burial (Tosafot and Ran Mo'ed Katan 23b).
and does not bless. The blessing of ha-motzi before the meal.
and does not invite. The Grace after Meals after the meal (Rashi Berakhot there).
and they do not bless for him. He does not need others to bless on his behalf to fulfill his obligation.
and they do not invite for him. He does not join the zimun (there).

and is exempt from reciting the Shema etc.. Out of respect for the dead and because he is preoccupied with the mitzvah of burying him (Meiri there 18a; and see also Hilchot Kriyat Shema 4:3, which explains that one who digs the grave and one who guards the dead are also exempt).
and from all the commandments. Positive commandments, but he is forbidden to do prohibitions.
except for marital relations. That he is not obligated to fulfill the mitzvah of onah, but if he wishes he may (Lechem Mishneh, Yad Peshutah).
not to become satiated. He should not drink a great deal, which could lead to drunkenness and distract him from the mourning (see also below 13:8).

they hasten his bier immediately. They hurry to bring his bier to burial, so as not to burden the public too much (Rabbeinu Yitzchak Gei'at, Hilchot Evel p. 232, and for other reasons see Beit Yosef).
and for his father and mother it is disgraceful. For out of respect for them he should prolong their eulogy and funeral.
it was the eve of Shabbat or the eve of a festival. And there is no time to delay and prolong the eulogy and funeral.
rains are pouring. Falling.
permitted. To hurry the burial of his father and mother.
one who leaves his dead overnight. Leaves him without burial.

transgresses a negative commandment. For it is said regarding those executed by the court: “you shall not leave his body overnight on the tree, but you shall surely bury him that day” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the Sages learned that the law is not only for those executed by the court, but for all the dead (Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:7-8, and see there and below 12:1 that there is also a positive commandment to bury the dead on the day of death).
and he is obligated to sit on an overturned bed. An upside-down bed (and see also below 5:18).
a mat. A rush mat.

for it is said in Ezekiel... implying that all the people are forbidden. When God informed Ezekiel that his wife would be taken by a plague, He commanded him not to follow the customs of mourning, and from there the Sages learned what the mourning customs are that a mourner generally must observe.
your glory. "Glory" is a term for tefillin (see Bavli Berakhot 11a).

implying that all the people eat from others' food on the first day and are forbidden to eat from their own. Thereby the mourner will not occupy himself with preparing food and be distracted from the mourning, and since others are commanded to feed him, they will naturally look after his needs, support him and comfort him.
on the first day by Torah law. For the mourning customs on the day of death and burial are from the Torah (as above 1:1).
to have a haircut. To get a haircut.
and to set the bed upright. Rather he must overturn all the beds in the mourner's house (as below, halachah 18).
and to let his head go bare. Rather he must cover his head (as below, halachah 19).

for He warned the sons of Aaron: “do not let your heads go bare”. After the death of Nadav and Avihu, God warned their brothers Elazar and Itamar not to behave by growing their hair, and from this the Sages learned that a mourner grows his hair and does not cut it.
and any hair he has. Even hair in covered places.
both the one who shaves and the one who is shaved. He is forbidden to remove his hair, whether himself or by others.
mustache. Moustache.

for it is said: “please mourn” etc.. Joab son of Zeruiah commands the wise woman to pretend to be a mourning woman, and the verse concludes: “and be like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for many days” (II Samuel 14:2).
and put on mourning garments. From here it is learned that a mourner must wear unlaundered garments.

and washing is included in anointing, since washing precedes anointing. Although the verse speaks only of anointing, since anointing is the last stage of washing, it is understood that washing is also forbidden.
garments. Clothes.

new and pressed white ones. But colored garments, even if new and pressed, a mourner is permitted to wear, because their newness and pressing do not significantly affect their appearance (see Meiri Mo'ed Katan 23a). Likewise new white garments that are not pressed, or old white garments even if pressed, a mourner is permitted to wear.

and pressed. Garments that were smoothed and straightened of wrinkles (Aruch, entry "gahatz"; Radbaz). Some explain that it refers to a stronger cleaning process than laundering, such as in hot water or with strong cleansers (Nimukei Yosef Mo'ed Katan 14b, and see Meiri there 23a).
and if it is to remove filth it is permitted. For they forbade only anointing for pleasure.
but in cold water he washes his face, hands and feet. For this is not washing for pleasure.
for it is said: “and David comforted Bathsheba” etc.. After the death of their child, at the end of the seven days of mourning (see Meiri Mo'ed Katan 15a).
and it is permitted to be alone with his wife though he is forbidden marital relations. And we do not suspect that he will have relations with her.
for it is said in Ezekiel etc.. See above 4:9 in the commentary.
if he was coming on the road, he wears shoes and goes. So that his feet are not injured (see also Hilchot Ta'aniyot 3:4).
and when he enters the city. When he enters the town.
and to go from town to town for trade. To travel from city to city for his business.
all the first three days. Which are the strongest part of mourning (Yerushalmi Mo'ed Katan 3:5).
and the woman spins with a spindle inside her house. A poor woman is permitted to spin with a spindle in her house (Ritva Mo'ed Katan 21b).

the things permitted to do on chol ha-moed. Work is forbidden on chol ha-moed. But work that, if not done, would cause a great loss, he is permitted to do, provided it does not involve great effort (see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:2-3).
his olives to turn. Before extracting the oil, the olives are placed in a pile to soften them, and they must be turned from time to time so they do not spoil from the heat generated in the pile.
and his jars to seal. For the opening of the barrels must be sealed after the wine or oil is put into them.
and his flax to take out of the soaking. For the raw flax placed in soaking water to soften it must be taken out so it does not rot in it.
and his wool from the pot. For the wool placed in a boiling pot for dyeing must be taken out, for if it stays there a long time it will spoil.
and they water lightly. They water with slight irrigation.

once the season of water arrives. For before sowing they water the field a little, and if they do not water it in this season and the rainy days come, the field will not be properly sown this year (Ramban Torat ha-Adam, the matter of mourning).
the sharecroppers. A sharecropper receives the field from its owner for a percentage of the crop.
and the lessees. A lessee receives the field from its owner for a fixed amount of produce.
and the contractors. The contractor mentioned here is one who pays fixed rent for the field in money (Meiri Mo'ed Katan 11b, and see Ritva, who explained differently).
these may work as they usually do. Because their work in the field is for themselves and they lose if they do not engage in it, they may work in it even when its owner becomes a mourner.

but the donkey drivers and camel drivers with his animals... these may not work. When they were not hired for a fixed time, it is a day-to-day hire, and although they work for themselves, since they can hire from someone else without loss they may not work with the mourner's animals or ship.

and if they were leased or hired earlier for a fixed time, these may work. For in a hire for a fixed time, the lessees will lose if they hire from another, and because they work for themselves, it is permitted (see Meiri there, and see the Rishonim there who explained this law in other ways).
a day laborer. One who works for the mourner in his field and receives a daily wage.
even in another city he may not do work for him. For work in the field is well known, and it is evident that he is working for the mourner (Radbaz, based on what is implied from below, halachah 13).
